items.question: A reviewer sees the while loop nested inside the for loop and rejects the solution as O(n²). Are they right?
items.answer: No. The inner while only runs when the window must shrink, and left never moves backwards. Across the whole run each unit is inserted into the Set at most once and removed at most once, so the combined work of both loops is bounded by a constant per unit and the algorithm is O(n). The linear bound comes from the monotonic pointers, not from the shape of the loops.
items.trap: The naive analysis multiplies the loop counts (n outer times n inner) and assumes the worst case repeats on every iteration. That reasoning is only valid when the inner loop can restart from scratch each time; here every shrink was prepaid by an earlier insertion, so the inner loop's total work across the entire run is at most n removals and the cost amortizes to linear.

items.question: The search box now receives emoji with modifiers, where one user-perceived character is several code points. Does Array.from(text) make the function count what users call a character?
items.answer: Not by itself. Array.from(text) iterates Unicode code points, which is already the safer choice over direct string indexing, which yields UTF-16 code units and splits surrogate pairs. But a grapheme cluster can span several code points (joined by zero-width joiners and modifiers), so one perceived character may occupy multiple positions in the window. Clarify with the interviewer which unit of uniqueness the product means (code units, code points, or grapheme clusters) and whether matching is case-sensitive before coding.
items.trap: The common answer treats 'character' as unambiguous and silently picks one unit. Direct indexing is wrong for astral-plane units (two code units per code point), and code points are still wrong for grapheme clusters (several code points per perceived character); assuming all three notions coincide is exactly the trap.

items.question: A teammate suggests replacing the whole function with [...new Set(records)]. Why does that silently fail for records merged from paginated responses?
items.answer: Because Set membership uses SameValueZero, and for objects that means identity: values are compared by reference, not by structure (MDN Set, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set). Each page is parsed separately, so the same record on two pages becomes two different object literals; neither equals the other, both are kept, and the spread returns the input with every duplicate intact. That is why the working version collects ids in a Set and filters by that explicit key.
items.trap: The naive assumption is that Set compares objects by contents the way it compares strings. It does not; only the exact same reference (or equal primitives) dedupes, so the one-liner looks like it works while every duplicate survives.

items.question: Product changes the rule to last record wins, but each id must stay at the position where it was first seen. How does the approach change?
items.answer: Switch from a Set of ids to a Map<string, RecordItem> keyed by id. On each record, map.set(id, record) replaces the value of an existing key, and Map iteration follows the order in which each key was first inserted (MDN Map, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map), so [...map.values()] yields last-wins values in first-seen positions. State the conflict rule (first wins, last wins, or merge) before coding, because it changes the data structure, not just a line.
items.trap: The common fix keeps the Set and overwrites entries in the output array by scanning for the existing id, which turns an O(n) pass into O(n²) and needs index bookkeeping. Others assume re-setting a Map key moves it to the end, so they rebuild the order manually and introduce the exact bug they were asked to avoid.

items.question: The indexed queue pushes every node and never removes anything; head just advances. A reviewer calls that a memory leak and proposes shift() to keep the array small. What is actually going on?
items.answer: It is not a leak; it is bounded scratch space. The array holds at most the visited nodes, O(v), and becomes garbage as soon as traversal finishes. The head index exists to avoid shift(), whose removal cost is linear in the remaining array; using it would make a large traversal pay quadratic queue costs. Trading transient O(v) scratch memory for quadratic time is a bad deal, and shift() does not even free the entries meaningfully, it reindexes the remainder.
items.trap: The naive reasoning equates 'an array that grows' with 'a leak' and reaches for shift() to free entries. shift() adds the linear copy cost back (reintroducing the exact problem the head index avoids) while saving nothing that matters, since the scratch array is unreachable right after the traversal returns.

items.question: The traversal matches selectors against node.children. What does it silently never see, and why does that matter for 'visible item labels'?
items.answer: children contains only element children, so text nodes are invisible to it, and it does not cross shadow-root boundaries, so shadow content is skipped. It also says nothing about layout visibility: an element can match [role=menuitem] while hidden by CSS or by an ancestor. The guidance is to define, before implementing, whether hidden subtrees, text nodes, shadow roots, and dynamically-added nodes are part of the traversal contract.
items.trap: The common answer treats DOM traversal as a solved generic problem: it confuses children with childNodes (assuming 'all children' are visited) and assumes matching a selector implies being visible. Both assumptions pass tests on a simple fixture and miss real menu content in production.

items.question: Your memoize closes over a Map keyed by the argument. Callers keep the same array reference and mutate its contents between calls. What does the cache do, and why?
items.answer: It returns the stale cached result. The Map key is the argument's identity, and identity has not changed, so the lookup hits even though the data behind the reference is different. This is the documented failure mode of an identity-keyed cache: mutable inputs can change after caching. The fix is a contract, not a hack: prefer immutable inputs, or make the key an explicit version or token that represents every input affecting the result.
items.trap: The naive expectation is that Map hashes the contents of the array, the way hash maps are imagined from other languages. Map keys use identity-based equality, so mutation is invisible to the cache and the UI silently shows old data; the cache hit makes it fast and wrong, which is worse than slow and right.

items.question: Product asks you to memoize the filtering so the first search feels instant too. What is wrong with the request, and what do you offer instead?
items.answer: Memoization only avoids repeating work for inputs it has already seen; it does not make the first computation cheaper, so a cold query is exactly as slow as before. It is also not a substitute for rendering only the rows that are needed: if the derived list still renders thousands of rows, caching the array saves computation but not rendering. Offer instead: measure before adding a cache, bound it when inputs like free-text queries are unbounded so stale keys cannot retain large results, and pair it with row-level rendering limits.
items.trap: The trap is treating memoization as a general 'make it fast' tool. It is a cache with memory and invalidation costs; on first-run workloads it delivers none of the promised speedup, and on unbounded-key workloads it adds stale-entry risk on top.

items.question: Fast typists complain that debounced search feels laggy: results only appear after they stop typing. What knob is missing, and what must be specified before adding it?
items.answer: A plain trailing debounce has exactly one knob, the wait, so a long burst delays the first result until the burst ends. The missing pieces from the production contract are leading versus trailing behavior and a maximum wait: a leading edge fires early in the burst, and a maxWait bounds how long a continuous burst can postpone the trailing call. Decide and document which edges fire, keep argument and this forwarding, expose cancellation, and treat the actual numbers as a product decision rather than a universal constant.
items.trap: The common reflex is to lower the wait, which reintroduces the request spam the debounce was added to prevent, or to swap in a throttle without stating its contract. Both change semantics silently; the honest answer is that debounce versus throttle is a behavior choice (only the settled value versus at most one invocation per interval) and the burst problem needs an explicit leading/maxWait decision.

items.question: You debounce a scroll handler that reads layout and writes styles. The call rate drops, but frames still jank. Why didn't the debounce help?
items.answer: Because rate limiting and frame alignment are different problems. Timer callbacks are ordinary tasks; a debounced callback runs whenever its timer fires, not synchronized with frames, so reads and writes can still interleave badly between frames. For visual scroll work the guidance is to keep the event handler light and batch the read/write work in requestAnimationFrame, so reads happen before writes inside a frame-aligned callback. Debounce may still be right for expensive non-visual work, but a timer alone does not guarantee frame-aligned rendering.
items.trap: The trap is believing that fewer calls equals well-timed calls. A debounced handler that fires mid-frame can still cause layout thrash; the fix is about when the work runs (a requestAnimationFrame batch), not only how often.

items.question: structuredClone() throws DataCloneError on your state object. A teammate says: just fall back to JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)). What is wrong with that fallback?
items.answer: The throw is telling you the value graph leaves structured-cloneable data: functions, many DOM nodes, or instances with behavior are not cloneable by the platform algorithm. The JSON round trip does not clone those either; it is serialization, so it silently loses or transforms values instead of failing loudly: function-valued and undefined properties are omitted, Map and Set entries are dropped (they stringify to {}), Date objects come back as strings, and cycles throw their own TypeError (MDN JSON.stringify, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/JSON/stringify). The fallback trades a loud, debuggable error for silent data corruption. The right move is to define the supported value graph and either scope the state to cloneable data or write a deliberately scoped clone.
items.trap: The naive framing is that structuredClone is strict and JSON is lenient, so JSON is the safe fallback. Leniency here means silent loss: the fallback passes a smoke test and corrupts state in production, and it still throws on the very cycles structuredClone would have handled.

items.question: Tests pass with a JSON round trip clone, but production state contains a Map and a self-reference. What exactly happens in each approach?
items.answer: structuredClone makes a deep copy that preserves the circular reference (the copy's self-pointer targets the copy, which is what the assertion copy.self === copy checks) and keeps the Map as a real Map. The JSON round trip cannot represent cycles, so it throws a TypeError, and it reduces the Map to an empty plain object, so the cloned state silently loses the filters. If the contract really is plain JSON only, serialization can be acceptable; the bug is applying it to state that is not plain JSON.
items.trap: The trap is extrapolating from tests: a fixture without Maps or cycles round trips fine, so the JSON clone looks equivalent. The two algorithms only agree on the plain-JSON subset of the value graph; outside it one throws or transforms, and 'passes tests' says nothing about the shapes production actually holds.

items.question: One of the three fetches rejects and Promise.all rejects immediately. Are the other two requests cancelled?
items.answer: No. Promise.all's rejection only abandons waiting for the remaining promises; the operations behind them keep running to completion, consuming bandwidth and resolving into nothing. Cancellation is a separate mechanism: pass one AbortSignal to every fetch and call abort() on route change or cleanup, and treat the resulting AbortError as expected rather than an error to surface. Concurrency (Promise.all), cancellation (AbortController), and failure handling are three different concerns.
items.trap: The phrase 'fail fast' suggests the sibling operations stop too. They do not: rejection is observation, not control. Code written under that assumption leaks in-flight requests, and the team wonders why the network waterfall persists after an 'abort' refactor that never actually aborted anything.

items.question: You add an isMounted guard before every state update, so an unmounted component can never update. Is the stale-result problem solved?
items.answer: No, that only covers the unmount case. The classic race happens while the component is still mounted: the user moves from route A to route B (or types a new query), B's faster response renders, then A's slower response lands and overwrites it. The guard that fixes this is request identity: tag each load with a version, id, or the latest signal, and apply only results whose identity is still current. Lifecycle guards and identity guards solve different halves; AbortSignal-based cancellation reduces how often the race happens but does not replace the identity check.
items.trap: The trap is treating 'don't update after unmount' as the whole race story. It covers the visible crash half; the silent wrong-data half (an old response beating a new one on a live component) is untouched by isMounted and is exactly the bug users report as the list flashing back to the old filter.

items.question: A queueMicrotask callback schedules another microtask, which schedules another, forever. The page freezes. Why does such tiny work kill the UI?
items.answer: Because of the drain rule, not the size of each callback. After the current task finishes, the browser drains the entire microtask queue before returning to the event loop; if draining keeps enqueueing more microtasks, the drain never ends, so no timer, input event, or rendering opportunity is ever reached. Each individual callback can be trivial and the interface still starves. Keep microtasks short, yield between chunks of CPU work, and use task or frame-aligned scheduling for large or visual work.
items.trap: The naive analysis counts cost per callback (each one is microseconds) and concludes microtasks are always safe. The starvation comes from the unbounded drain-before-render rule: one self-perpetuating chain is enough to defer input and paint indefinitely, regardless of how small each step is.

items.question: A teammate wraps 'run after the screen updates' in setTimeout(..., 0), arguing the browser must have painted by then. Why is that wrong?
items.answer: Scheduling order and paint guarantees are different things. What the event loop promises is that microtasks scheduled during the current task run before the next task, so a promise callback can run before a zero-delay timer; it does not promise that a paint happened in between. A setTimeout callback can execute before the browser next renders, so 'timer means painted' is unfounded. For work that must be frame-aligned, use a frame-aligned scheduling strategy such as requestAnimationFrame rather than inferring paint state from timer order.
items.trap: The trap is reading 'setTimeout 0 runs later' as 'runs after everything, including paint'. Zero delay only means 'after the current task and its microtasks, when a timer task is picked'; whether a paint occurred in between is unspecified, so code that measures layout or assumes visible state can run against a stale frame.

items.question: A teammate simplifies your walker by returning FILTER_SKIP for [data-private] elements instead of FILTER_REJECT. Private text now leaks into the output. Why?
items.answer: For a TreeWalker, FILTER_REJECT on a node rejects the node and its entire subtree, while FILTER_SKIP skips only the node itself and still descends into its children. The original code relies on REJECT precisely so a private element's descendants are excluded; with SKIP, the walker does not report the private element but happily walks into it and accepts its text nodes. The distinction is real for TreeWalker; for NodeIterator the two constants are documented as equivalent and children are still visited (MDN, https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/createNodeIterator).
items.trap: The names sound interchangeable (skip it versus reject it), and on nodes without children, like text nodes, the difference is invisible, so tests on flat content pass. The trap is assuming the filter constants are stylistic synonyms; for elements with subtrees they are the difference between pruning a branch and pruning a single node.

items.question: The requirement changes from subtrees marked data-private to anything the user cannot currently see. Does the TreeWalker still apply?
items.answer: Not as-is. TreeWalker filters see node type and attributes; they do not answer visual visibility. An element can be invisible via CSS (for example display: none on an ancestor), have zero size, or sit outside a clipped area, and the walker will still report its text. Visual visibility requires layout information, such as computed styles or intersection checks, which is a different mechanism with its own cost. Also re-clarify the other boundaries the contract must state: shadow roots, live mutations during traversal, and whitespace-only text nodes.
items.trap: The trap is assuming 'filtering the DOM' is one problem. Attribute-based pruning and layout-based visibility are different data sources; a walker that is correct for data-private can be completely wrong for 'not visible', and mixing them silently produces both false positives (hidden text kept) and false negatives.

items.question: Your mapWithLimit rejects on the first worker error. When item 7 fails, what happens to the tasks already in flight, and is that cancellation?
items.answer: Promise.all stops awaiting the other workers, but their tasks keep running: the operations behind them were already started and rejection does not reach them, so in-flight work is merely observed, not cancelled, and its results are never used. The design must state the failure contract explicitly: fail fast (reject and leave started tasks to finish unobserved), per-item outcomes (an allSettled-style report), or active cancellation by threading an AbortSignal into tasks and aborting on first failure. Fail fast and cancel the rest are different guarantees.
items.trap: The trap is the phrase 'fail fast' implying the scheduler stops the work. It only stops the waiting. Teams discover this when the 'cancelled' batch still saturates the network: nothing was cancelled, the mapper just stopped listening.

items.question: Why does the implementation spawn Math.min(limit, items.length) workers that pull indices, instead of simply starting all the tasks at once?
items.answer: Because starting all tasks at once is exactly Promise.all(items.map(task)), the unbounded pattern the utility exists to prevent: every fetch or metadata read would be in flight immediately, defeating the caller-supplied limit. The worker-pool shape is the guarantee: at most limit tasks are active at any moment, each worker pulls the next index when it settles, and results land at their original index so output order is preserved despite different completion order. The min() avoids spawning workers for an empty or short list. The limit protects browser and server resources; it does not by itself guarantee throughput or make individual tasks faster.
items.trap: The trap is reading the worker loop as a style choice or micro-optimization. It is the core invariant: without it the limit is decorative. A related misconception is that limiting concurrency speeds tasks up or guarantees network throughput; it only caps simultaneous resource use.

mcqs.question: The sliding-window solution for the longest substring without repeating characters uses two indices and a Set. What is its time complexity, and why?
options: O(n): each unit is inserted into the Set at most once and removed at most once, so the total work of both loops together is bounded by a constant per unit.
O(n²): a while loop is nested inside the for loop, so the worst case is n times n iterations.
O(n log n): Set operations cost log n on average and there are n of them.
O(min(n, distinct units)): the running time matches the Set's size bound.
mcqs.explanation: Correct because the left index never moves backwards: every shrink of the window consumes work that was prepaid by an earlier insertion, so each unit is added and removed at most once and the nested shape still amortizes to O(n). The strongest distractor is option 1: multiplying loop counts is only valid when the inner loop can restart from scratch on every outer iteration, which the monotonic left pointer makes impossible. Option 3 quotes the space bound, O(min(n, distinct-unit-count)), not the time bound.

mcqs.question: For a search box that may receive multi-code-point emoji, what does Array.from(text) give the longest-unique-substring algorithm, and what does it still not give?
options: Unicode code points, one per element; it does not segment grapheme clusters, so one user-perceived character can occupy several elements.
UTF-16 code units, exactly like direct string indexing, so surrogate pairs are split into two elements.
Grapheme clusters, one per user-perceived character, because Array.from splits text on perceived boundaries.
The same count as text.length: both count UTF-16 code units, so the choice cannot change the result.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Array.from iterates code points, the safe default over raw indexing, but an emoji with a skin-tone modifier or a ZWJ sequence is several code points, so grapheme-level uniqueness needs a separate segmentation step and must be clarified as a requirement. The strongest distractor is option 2, which overcredits Array.from: it stops at code points and knows nothing about user-perceived boundaries. Option 1 describes direct string indexing, and option 3 wrongly assumes text.length counts what Array.from yields.

mcqs.question: Records arrive from several paginated responses, each parsed separately, so the same record can appear as two distinct objects. Which implementation dedupes by id, keeps the first-seen record and its position, and runs in O(n) average time?
options: return [...new Set(records)]: Set stores unique values and iterates in insertion order.
Filter with a Set of ids: skip a record whose id is already present, otherwise add the id and keep the record.
Sort the records by id, then remove adjacent duplicates.
Filter with a nested scan: keep a record only if no previously kept record has the same id.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: an explicit stable key (id) with Set membership gives O(n) average time and preserves first-seen order, which is exactly the bank's pattern. The strongest distractor is option 0: everything stated about Set is true (unique values, insertion order), but membership uses identity-based equality, so two separately created object literals with identical fields are both kept and nothing is deduped. Option 2 breaks the first-seen-position requirement and costs O(n log n); option 3 produces correct output but degrades to O(n²) on large merges.

mcqs.question: In a large breadth-first DOM traversal, why does the queue use a head index that only advances, instead of Array.shift()?
options: shift() removes from the wrong end for a FIFO queue, so the traversal order would become depth-first.
shift() is deprecated and scheduled for removal from the language.
shift()'s removal cost is linear in the remaining array, so a large traversal pays quadratic queue costs; the head index makes each dequeue O(1).
Arrays cannot shrink once allocated, so shift() only nulls the first slot and leaks it.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: shift() reindexes every remaining element, so removing n items one at a time costs O(n²) in queue operations; keeping a head index makes each dequeue O(1) and the whole traversal O(v + e). The strongest distractor is option 0: shift() is the correct FIFO end semantically, the problem is purely its cost, and confusing the two would point the fix in the wrong direction. Option 3 invents a memory model; shift() copies the remainder, it does not just null a slot.

mcqs.question: Which statement about memoizing an expensive derived value for a filterable list is correct?
options: Memoization makes the first computation cheaper by caching partial results during the initial run.
A Map keyed by the argument's identity stays correct even if callers mutate the argument between calls, because Map re-hashes the contents on lookup.
Memoization avoids repeating work for inputs already seen; it does not make the first computation cheaper and does not replace rendering only the rows that are needed.
An unbounded cache is safe for free-text query keys because Map evicts stale entries with LRU behavior.
mcqs.explanation: Correct, and it is the bank's exact caution: a cache only pays off on repeated inputs, so cold queries are as slow as before, and caching a derived array does nothing about rendering thousands of DOM rows. The strongest distractor is option 1: Map keys use identity-based equality, so a mutated-but-same-reference argument is a cache hit that returns stale data; the key must represent every input affecting the result, via immutable inputs or explicit versioning. Option 3 invents eviction: Map has none, which is why unbounded keys must be bounded by design.

mcqs.question: Choose the rate-limiting tool: (1) a search box where only the settled query should hit the API; (2) a scroll handler where the UI should update at a regular cadence while scrolling continues. Which pairing is right?
options: Throttle the search and debounce the scroll.

Debounce the search and throttle the scroll: debounce waits until calls stop for the delay so only the settled query fires; throttle permits at most one invocation per interval so updates stay regular.
Debounce both: debounce is the stricter, more modern option and subsumes throttle.
Use requestAnimationFrame for both: rAF is a rate limiter with a configurable interval.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the definitions map directly onto the requirements; search needs the settled value (debounce waits until calls have stopped for the delay) and continuous scroll needs regular updates (throttle allows at most one invocation per interval). The strongest distractor is option 0, which inverts the criterion: it would hit the API on every keystroke bucket and starve scroll updates until scrolling stops entirely. Option 3 mislabels rAF: it aligns work with frames and has no configurable interval; the guidance is to batch scroll reads and writes in rAF in addition to keeping the handler light, not to use rAF as a debounce or throttle.

mcqs.question: Which set of values can structuredClone() copy in a browser but a JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) round trip cannot preserve?
options: A function and a live DOM element node.
A Map with entries, a circular reference, and a Date object.
A Promise and a WeakMap.
None: both approaches clone exactly the same value graph and differ only in speed.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: structuredClone makes a deep copy that preserves circular references and keeps structured-cloneable values like Maps intact, while the JSON round trip is serialization: Map and Set entries are dropped (they stringify to {}), Dates come back as strings, and cycles throw a TypeError. The strongest distractor is option 0: functions and many DOM nodes are precisely the values that make structuredClone throw DataCloneError, since it is not a universal clone. Option 3 misses that the two algorithms only agree on the plain-JSON subset of the value graph.

mcqs.question: A route runs three independent fetches under Promise.all and one rejects. What happens to the other two network requests?
options: They are cancelled automatically: Promise.all's rejection propagates to sibling promises.
They keep running to completion; the rejection only abandons waiting for them, and cancelling them requires an AbortSignal passed to each fetch.
They are paused until the rejection is handled, then resumed or cancelled by the handler.
They resolve normally but Promise.all discards their results, which amounts to the same thing as cancelling them.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Promise.all preserves input order and rejects on the first rejection, but rejection does not cancel the remaining operations; without signals the siblings still consume bandwidth and resolve into nothing. The strongest distractor is option 3: it is half right (their results are indeed discarded) and draws the wrong conclusion, since the requests still complete and the wasted work is observable on the network. Option 0 is the classic conflation of fail-fast observation with cancellation, the exact mix-up of concurrency, cancellation, and stale-result protection the bank warns about.

mcqs.question: What is the output order of: console.log('task start'); queueMicrotask(() => console.log('microtask')); setTimeout(() => console.log('timer task'), 0); console.log('task end');?
options: task start, microtask, task end, timer task
task start, task end, timer task, microtask
task start, task end, microtask, timer task
task start, timer task, task end, microtask
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the two synchronous logs run first; after the current task finishes the browser drains the microtask queue before returning to the event loop, so the microtask runs before the zero-delay timer task, exactly the bank's example. The strongest distractor is option 0: it assumes queueMicrotask runs its callback inline at the enqueue point, which would make microtasks indistinguishable from synchronous code. Option 1 reverses the drain rule by letting a task (the timer) run before pending microtasks, and option 2 treats setTimeout(..., 0) as synchronous.

mcqs.question: In a TreeWalker, an element matches the private-subtree rule. What is the difference between returning FILTER_REJECT and FILTER_SKIP for that element?
options: REJECT excludes the element and its entire subtree; SKIP excludes only the element and still visits its children.
REJECT aborts the whole traversal with an error; SKIP is the safe non-throwing variant.
They are equivalent for elements; the constants only differ for text and comment nodes.
SKIP excludes the element's subtree while REJECT excludes only the element itself.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the bank's walker returns FILTER_REJECT for a private element precisely so its descendants are excluded, while non-target elements get FILTER_SKIP so traversal still descends into them. The strongest distractor is option 3, which inverts the semantics and would leak private text exactly like the naive simplification. Option 2 is plausible because the two constants do behave the same for NodeIterator (children are still visited), but for TreeWalker the subtree pruning is the entire point of REJECT.

scenarios.prompt: A dashboard route runs loadDashboard() on entry, may unmount before the fetches finish, and can be re-entered quickly. (1) Name every correctness and efficiency problem in this code. (2) Rewrite it so the three resources load concurrently, obsolete results can never render, and navigation cancels work. (3) State what changes if partial data is useful.
rubric: Identifies the waterfall: independent operations awaited one by one instead of started together, so latency sums.
Uses Promise.all for all-or-nothing loading and can state its exact semantics: preserves input order, rejects on first rejection, does not cancel the remaining operations.
Adds cancellation: one AbortSignal passed to every fetch, abort() on route change and cleanup, AbortError treated as expected rather than an error.
Guards rendering with request identity (current controller or version), so a slower obsolete load cannot overwrite newer data even while the component is still mounted.
Knows the partial-data alternative: Promise.allSettled with per-outcome rendering, and checks response.ok before parsing.

scenarios.prompt: This utility ships in a widget bundle. (1) List every defect in debounce and in how it is applied to the search input and the scroll badge. (2) Write a production version and spell out its API contract. (3) Explain what to do differently for the scroll badge and on component teardown.
rubric: Spots that arguments (and this) are dropped: the trailing call invokes fn with none of the handler's values.
Adds cancel() clearing the timer and requires calling it on teardown so no trailing call survives unmount and the closure stops retaining stale work.
States the leading/trailing and maxWait decisions explicitly instead of silently shipping trailing-only, and treats the interval as a product decision.
For the scroll badge, replaces timer-only debouncing with a light handler plus requestAnimationFrame-batched read/write: frame alignment, not just call rate.
Can justify debounce for search (only the settled query matters) versus throttle for continuous scroll, resize, or pointer work (at most one invocation per interval).

scenarios.prompt: mergePages combines users from several paginated API responses; the same user can appear on more than one page, and each page is parsed separately, so duplicates are distinct objects. (1) Explain precisely why the current implementation removes nothing. (2) Rewrite it so the last-seen record wins while every id stays at the position where it was first seen. (3) State the complexity and what you would ask the product owner first.
rubric: Explains the identity-versus-structural failure precisely: Set keeps both separately parsed objects because object values compare by reference, not by structure.
Keys by the stable id and states the conflict rule (last-wins here) before or while coding.
Knows Map re-set semantics: the value is replaced while the key keeps its first-insertion position, yielding last-wins values in first-seen order.
States O(n) average time and O(n) additional space, and avoids sort-then-dedupe, which breaks first-seen order and costs O(n log n).

scenarios.prompt: The team uses this to prefetch a list of pages with limit 3. A caller asserts that results arrive in input order and the assertion fails intermittently. (1) Explain the order bug and why it is intermittent. (2) The utility also silently misbehaves for some limit values and has an unstated failure contract; identify both. (3) Fix the code and write down the guarantees the fixed version gives.
rubric: Diagnoses the order bug: push-in-completion-order versus assignment at the original index, and explains the intermittency (it depends on task timing).
Preserves the at-most-limit invariant with the worker-pool pull loop rather than starting all tasks at once.
Validates the limit as a positive integer instead of silently returning wrong output for 0, negatives, or fractions.
States the failure contract: fail-fast rejection leaves in-flight tasks running (observed, not cancelled), or offers per-item outcomes or AbortSignal-based cancellation.
Notes what the limit does and does not promise: caps simultaneous resource use; no throughput guarantee, no faster individual tasks.
